title: Muzychuk Wins Blitz Portion Of WR Women's Chess Tour Grand Final
summary:
GM Anna Muzychuk won the blitz portion of the WR Women's Chess Tour - Grand Final 2026 after defeating GM Kateryna Lagno 2.5-1.5 in the Final. Muzychuk leads the event, but there is a full rapid knockout tournament to go.

The second and final day of the event is on Monday, November 23, starting at 5:00 a.m. ET / 11:00 CET / 3:30 p.m. IST.

Blitz Bracket

Image: Courtesy of WR Chess.

The WR Women's Chess Tour - Grand Final 2026 is the last event of a five-month tournament series. The inaugural tour started in Japan (in June), moved to the Dominican Republic (in July), Mozambique (at the end of August), and France (at the end of August). Two players qualified from each of the four events to create a Grand Final with eight players who represent some of the strongest women on earth.

GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, who qualified by winning the rapid section in France, declined her invitation to the Grand Final to join GM Javokhir Sindarov for the 2026 FIDE World Chess Championship. She was replaced by GM Mariya Muzychuk, so both Muzychuk sisters are in the field.

The tournament takes place at the Rosenstein Palace in Stuttgart, Germany. The building was originally built as the summer palace for King Wilhelm I of Wurttemberg and now houses the State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart.

Photo: Wikipedia. By CatalpaSpirit - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The two-day event features blitz chess (3+2 time control) and rapid chess (15+10). On the first day, all players played a single-elimination knockout in blitz (best of four games in each match), and on the second day they will do the same thing but with rapid chess (best of two games in each match).

The overall Grand Final winner is the player with the most combined points from the blitz and rapid tournaments. In each tournament, players earn the following points according to the standings:

1st: 10 points

2nd: 8 points

3rd-4th: 5 points

5th-8th: 2 points

The total prize fund is $40,000, with $7,000 for first place.

Muzychuk couldn't pinpoint which match was hardest; they were all difficult to get through. The first round was especially "unpleasant," she said, as she had to play her sister, Mariya, before going on to defeat the top seed, GM Zhu Jiner, and then three-time Women's World Blitz Champion Kateryna Lagno.

Muzychuk vs. Lagno in the Final. Photo: WR Chess.

Quarterfinals: Muzychuk, Zhu, Garifullina, Lagno Advance

We start from the beginning. The Quarterfinals saw Anna defeat her sister, Mariya, 2.5-1.5 in the first match; Zhu beat IM Carissa Yip 1.5-2.5; IM Leya Garifullina beat IM Mai Narva 2.5-0-.5; and Lagno beat GM Vaishali Rameshbabu 2.5-0.5.

Mariya found it funny that she and Anna flew to Germany just to play each other when they could just as easily play blitz games at home. They don't often play decisive games, but a knockout format gave them no choice but to play for a win—just as we saw in the 2023 FIDE World Cup, where Anna also won their encounter. This match started with one draw, but the next three games were decisive, with Anna winning games two and four with the white pieces.

Anna came out on top in game four when her sister blundered the f-pawn. Knights are tricky pieces in blitz, and a few moves later, the same knight that won the pawn also trapped the rook on d3.

In another quarterfinal, Zhu defeated the American number-one woman Yip. Game one was a crucial swindle, as Yip was a piece up with a winning position. Trading rooks not only threw away the win but lost the game.

Despite the early knockout, Yip saw the positive side: at least now could now get boba.

"It always sucks to be knocked out early, but it's also good to finish early so now I can get my boba," says Carissa Yip. "I guess I'm also going to get boba," adds Mai Narva. https://t.co/Gaz1wDZEmZ

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 22, 2026

Garifullina won the first two games against Narva (Yip's boba partner), and then a drew in the third won the match with a game to spare.

Lagno also won her match in three games after taking full points in game one and three. Lagno's speed paid off: in game one, with four seconds against 29, Vaishali walked into a checkmating attack with 24.Kh2??. The only move 24.Ra4! was a big ask, given the time disadvantage.

Semifinals: Muzychuk, Lagno Advance

In the Semifinals, we saw Anna Muzychuk face Zhu and Lagno play against Garifullina. Muzychuk won game one, lost game two, and after a draw in game three she won the fourth and final game. That one looked sure to be a draw, a knight endgame with four pawns for each player, but Zhu played a tragic move that simply blundered a piece. This is some really bad luck:

Lagno, on the other hand, started by losing game one, but then winning games two and three. With a draw in game four, she won the match against Garifullina. The margin was close, as Garifullina was up a pawn and winning at one point in game two—and then, in an equal rook endgame, she lost on time. In game three, she resigned one move before checkmate.

Final: Muzychuk Wins

When Anna Muzychuk won the first two games against Lagno, it looked like a one-sided match might wrap up with a game to spare. In game one, Lagno played an unsound pawn sacrifice; in the game two time scramble, Lagno walked into a permanent pin and lost the exchange. The players—Muzychuk from Ukraine, Lagno from Russia—did not shake hands.

Game three brought intrigue back into the match as Muzychuk said she only thought about her plan and admitted she didn't pause to consider her opponent's—it happens in blitz. 16.Qd2 telegraphed the obvious: a deadly bishop sacrifice.

Still, Muzychuk had a second chance to win the match with a draw, and in game four she had the white pieces. They played the Four Knights, and by move 11 the queens were traded. Muzychuk was never in trouble and drew comfortably.

That gives Muzychuk 10 points and a two-point lead over Lagno ahead of the rapid portion. That begins seven hours earlier on Monday. As you can see in the pairings, if the Muzychuk sisters are toi play each other again, it won't happen again until the final match.

Image: Courtesy of WR Chess.

How to watch?

You can watch the event on the WR YouTube channel. The games can also be followed from our Events Page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM Elisabeth Paehtz.

The WR Women's Chess Tour - Grand Final 2026, held in Stuttgart, Germany on November 22 and 23, is the final event of the inaugural tournament series. The top eight qualifiers from the tour play in two single-elimination knockouts, one blitz tournament (3+2 time control) followed by a rapid one (15+10). The overall Grand Final winner is the player with the most combined points from the blitz and rapid tournaments. The prize fund is $40,000, with $7,000 for first place.

title: Sindarov Gets White As Gukesh Vows To Win World Championship 'All Over Again'
summary:
GM Javokhir Sindarov will start the 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship with the white pieces in Geneva on Tuesday after World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju selected a clock containing a black knight at the opening ceremony. Earlier, at the press conference, Sindarov noted how short his six months of preparation had seemed, while Gukesh, asked about defending his title, commented, "I don’t think I’m here to defend anything—I’m here to win it all over again!"

For the players, the key detail of the media day before the match is getting to know who will make the first move. That was decided in the opening ceremony that took place Sunday in the impressive Palace of Nations. In Singapore in 2024, the colors for the first game of GM Ding Liren's match against Gukesh were decided in a dramatic laser display. This time, it was done in more understated Swiss style as Gukesh got to select from a pair of clocks—containing light or dark chocolate knights.

The moment @DGukesh picked a clock with a black chocolate knight inside and therefore starts with Black vs. @GMJSindarov in Tuesday's Game 1 of the 2026 FIDE World Championship! #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/57JyfsNY5z

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 22, 2026

Sindarov will now have the white pieces and make the first move in game one on Tuesday—the game starts at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST, and we'll have commentary from GMs Judit Polgar and David Howell—before Gukesh and Sindarov alternate colors for the remaining 13 games. The first rest day is on Friday, after three games have been played.

Sindarov was left with the white knight, meaning he gets White in game one. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

You can watch the full opening ceremony below.

The match itself will take place in the Fondation Martin Bodmer, a library and museum in Cologny, overlooking Lake Geneva, but the opening press conference was also held at the United Nations building, in the Kazakh room, hence the presence of the Kazakh ambassador as well as host GM Maurice Ashley and FIDE President Timur Turlov.

The opening press conference is a long-standing tradition. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

The players spent almost an hour talking about the match, and again, you can watch that below.

If you'd prefer to read, we've transcribed all the players' answers below:

How different is playing the World Championship as the reigning champion?

Gukesh: First of all, I’m really glad to be here, glad to be in Geneva for this match. I think compared to the last time it feels like I’m more experienced coming into the match, but whatever has happened till now just gets erased when we sit at the table for game one. It’s a completely different match, a completely different opponent, a different place, so I’m not really thinking about other things, just giving my best for these 14 games.

Whatever has happened till now just gets erased when we sit at the table for game one.

—Gukesh Dommaraju

I think Sindarov has just been in very consistent and very good form, and surely one of the very top players at the very top of his game, so it’s for sure going to be a real test, but I have prepared the best way that I can and I’m very enthusiastic for this match—to test myself against such a strong player and to see what I’m capable of.

How have the last six months since winning the Candidates been?

Sindarov: After Cyprus, I played a lot of tournaments in a row, and this six months, I was thinking I have a lot of time, but it passed very fast. I was traveling a lot, I played many tournaments. Today I’m here, I’m very happy to fight for this crown, and I’ll try to enjoy the match. I know it will be very hard. It’s my first experience, and we’ll see. But anyway, I’m happy—many chess players play their whole life in chess and they don’t have a chance to play for this, so I’m happy that today I have a chance to fight for this.

Many chess players play their whole life in chess and they don't have a chance to play for this.

—Javokhir Sindarov

Javokhir Sindarov has a chance of a lifetime. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

What do you expect from Gukesh?

Sindarov: Gukesh’s performance in 2024 is something fantastic and we already know he played very well. Of course, if you took his last year, he’s unlucky, but still, this year I played against him in Tata Steel, and I feel he’s really very strong. Sometimes you have bad periods, but I think it doesn’t mean a lot, because like we saw with Ding also in 2024, he played very bad tournaments, but still in the match he played well. I don’t think we need to think about all of this stuff. I’m just trying to play against a strong opponent and trying to enjoy the match.

Is the role of defending a title more difficult?

Gukesh: I don’t think I’m here to defend anything—I’m here to win it all over again! That’s the mindset I’m in.

I don’t think I’m here to defend anything—I’m here to win it all over again!

—Gukesh Dommaraju

Gukesh has had a tough couple of years, but was in fine form in the press conference. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

How do you rate your chances?

Sindarov: I’ve had many interviews about this, but I think I’ll say the chances are 50:50. I don’t want to say anything, because the match will be very tough. It’s normal to give 50:50, because it’s a hard match, 14 games, and anything can happen.

What will the players eat during the match?

Gukesh: I generally prefer just food that I’m comfortable with. Usually I eat a lot of Indian food. Some people in Geneva have been very kind to prepare food for me, so I’m getting home-cooked Indian food, which I’m very comfortable with. So I’m very grateful for it.

Sindarov: Actually I’m the guy who can eat any cuisine, it doesn’t matter, but here I’m happy. In Samarkand our team had a special chef who made for us every day food. Our government was also bringing some chefs from Uzbekistan, but as I said, I’m really happy to have any food, and if I want to go after Sunday to some Japanese cuisine, I’m really happy to go, so for me especially it doesn’t really matter a lot. I’m happy with everything.

Why did Sindarov play so much before the match, and did it surprise Gukesh?

Sindarov: We talked about this a little bit with Roman [Vidonyak, his coach]. First, I had an invitation from the Grand Chess Tour before I won the Candidates, and of course when you get to play such a strong tournament, when you have the opportunity, I immediately agreed to play. My goal even after I won the Candidates was to have more experience, because I didn’t play that many strong tournaments in my career. From this year probably I really start playing such strong tournaments as Tata Steel, so that’s why I chose to play many tournaments, and I’m happy with my decision.

I didn't play that many strong tournaments in my career.

—Javokhir Sindarov

Gukesh: Not really. Me and my team kind of expected that he’ll play more than me. We had decided to slow down the tournaments quite a bit this year, but basically the same reason that Sindarov has said, that this is kind of the first year that he’s been playing at the very elite, and we just thought that it made sense that he’ll make use of the good momentum and he’ll get more experience against the top guys. It was not a surprise at all.

What were the players looking for when inspecting the library playing hall?

Gukesh: I checked the playing hall yesterday. It was basically checking whether I’ll be able to feel comfortable for four-five hours every day. I checked the chairs, the lighting, the floors, different kinds of things that can bother you during a game. But I was happy with pretty much everything, and about the books—I just saw there were a lot of books. I didn’t really bother to check what books they are. I don’t think I’ll be reading in between the games!

😉 Every detail matters! Javokhir Sindarov picks his chair for the biggest match of his career so far! ♟ Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 🇮🇳 Gukesh D 🆚 Javokhir Sindarov 🇺🇿 📍 Geneva, Switzerland 🇨🇭 🗓 Games: November 24 – December 12, 2026 PURCHASE YOUR TICKETS HERE: https://t.co/PHVEOZwyAH #GukeshSindarov

— International Chess Federation (@FIDE_chess) November 21, 2026

Sindarov: It’s my first time that there’s nobody playing around us, only us. It can be boring sometimes, because you don’t know who to watch, because even in some other tournaments when I played, there should be someone who I always watch, but in general we looked at the rooms, everything. The playing hall is really very beautiful. I was thinking I’ll play in a box, but still it looks very fine, and I hope for a great match.

How was Sindarov’s training camp in October in Cyprus?

Sindarov: It was a great memory. I came back after the Candidates for the Cap St Georges Hotel and I want to say my thanks for the managers of the hotel. We had a great camp there. Somehow I met Hikaru there also. He was also taking a rest; he said he’s preparing for Clutch Chess, but in general I have a very good rest there and good preparation and our team was happy, so I’m really happy and maybe soon I’ll come back to this place.

Many astute observers have noted that @GMJSindarov and I are at the same hotel in Cyprus for the same dates, and they're questioning if I'm on Sindarov's World Championship Prep Team. While I'm not, I am advising him in a limited capacity about 2.Ke2. The OG prep was for an eventual WC match against Magnus, but as that won't be happening, the world deserves to have this prep in the open, so I'm sharing it. I've also heard that Magnus is sharing his 2.Ke2 prep with @DGukesh. Good Luck to Sindarov and Gukesh, may the best 2.Ke2 win!

— Hikaru Nakamura (@GMHikaru) October 15, 2026

Can the players reveal their seconds?

Gukesh: I’m here with Gaju, and other team members I would like to reveal later.

Sindarov: In my team here there’s Roman, and everybody knows Mukhiddin Madaminov is also here, and also Nikita Vitiugov is helping me here. I have other teams, but maybe after the match I will show.

Sindarov's team in Geneva wasn't hiding, with GM Shamsiddin Vokhidov one player Sindarov didn't name in the press conference. Photo: Y. E. Nisenbaum/FIDE.

What changes has AI made in chess?

Sindarov: In my opinion in the last six years the engines have changed a lot. Sometimes it’s become boring to prep such long lines, because before engines were showing some lines are very bad, but now it’s completely different evaluation there. In my opinion, chess became stronger. In general, openings mean a lot, but still you have to play very good chess, but I will say from other matches 10 years ago that opening preparation has changed really a lot. That’s the main point right now.

Gukesh's arrival at the Palace of Nations. Photo: Y. E. Nisenbaum.

Gukesh: I guess the clear answer is that opening prep has become much more computer-based, and it’s very hard to disagree with the computers sometimes, but also, for example, the general level keeps rising the more people work with computers. They also learn a lot more ideas, not just opening ideas, but in general, they understand structures better. Defense gets better because the computer is always very resourceful. I think just working with computers has increased the level of chess by humans and made it much harder to win games, but also I think it makes it more of a sport. Everybody has access to similar things that help them like engines, seconds, coaches, but you need to find something that will help you be slightly better than the rest, which is what sport is about, I think.

I think it makes it more of a sport.

—Gukesh Dommaraju on the equalizing effect of AI in chess

How different is preparing for a single opponent?

Sindarov: The most different part of preparation, for Swiss tournaments, for small mini-matches, for a big match, it’s the opening. You need to work really a lot. I was thinking six months—I have enough time—but maybe even this six months, I played many tournaments, bu

title: FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Championships 2026: Media accreditation now open
summary: FIDE is pleased to announce the opening of media accreditation for the FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Championships 2026, one of the most exciting events on the international chess calendar. Held annually in both the Open and Women’s sections, the championships consistently attract the world’s strongest players, drawn by the prestige of the titles, a prize fund exceeding €1 million, and the unique festive atmosphere of this end-of-year event. Titles at stake: FIDE World Rapid Champion FIDE Women’s World Rapid Champion FIDE World Blitz Champion FIDE Women’s World Blitz Champion Dates: 25 December: Arrivals 26–28 December: FIDE World Rapid Championships 29–30 December: FIDE World Blitz Championships 31 December: Departures Location: WOW Convention Center, Istanbul, Türkiye Media Accreditation: We invite all media representatives wishing to cover the event to submit their accreditation applications via the media registration form: https://worldrapidandblitz.fide.com/media_registration Please note that there will be no on-site registration desk at the venue. The online form is the only way to obtain media accreditation. Once submitted, your application will be reviewed by our team. If approved, you will receive a separate confirmation email. Accreditation will remain open throughout the championship. However, we cannot guarantee timely processing of last-minute applications, so we strongly encourage media representatives to apply in advance. Press accreditation is reserved for professional journalists and media representatives working on behalf of bona fide media organisations. A limited number of accreditations may also be granted to independent writers, bloggers, YouTubers and freelance reporters. Accredited media representatives will be able to collect their badges onsite. A valid photo ID or travel document must be presented when collecting accreditation.The organisers will provide accredited media with dedicated working facilities and services to support comprehensive coverage of the championships. We look forward to welcoming media representatives to Istanbul and to sharing the excitement of the FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Championships 2026 with chess fans around the globe. Official website: https://worldrapidandblitz.fide.com/

title: World Championship Match 2026 opens in Geneva at a historic venue
summary: The Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 officially got underway this afternoon with an opening ceremony at the Palais des Nations in Geneva. It would be difficult to imagine a more fitting or prestigious setting for such an occasion. As H.E. Erzhan Kazykhan had pointed out during the press conference earlier in the day, FIDE’s motto, Gens una sumus («We are one family»), resonates particularly well with the spirit and ideals of the United Nations. The impressive Assembly Hall provided the stage for the ceremony, which was hosted by Maurice Ashley and Angelika Valkova. The programme brought together a series of short films, speeches by distinguished guests and artistic performances. Running through the entire event was a common theme: the rich tradition of World Championship matches and their place in chess history. The story of the World Championship could almost be read like a book, with each match adding a new chapter to an extraordinary legacy. Now, Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov are preparing to write new pages in a story that began 140 years ago. The literary metaphor was particularly apt, considering that the match itself will be held at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, an institution devoted to preserving and showcasing one of the world’s most remarkable collections of manuscripts and rare books. In a heartfelt address, Jacques Berthold, the Foundation’s outgoing Director, highlighted the enduring relationship between chess and literature, recalling how the game has inspired renowned authors and featured in numerous literary works, including some preserved in the Foundation’s own collections. Following a captivating live sand-art performance came one of the most eagerly anticipated moments of the ceremony: the drawing of colours for the first game. The reigning World Champion was invited to open one of two large Swiss clocks displayed on stage. Inside the one he chose was a beautifully crafted knight made of dark chocolate. His pick means that Javokhir Sindarov, who revealed the white-chocolate knight in the other clock, will have the white pieces when the match begins on Tuesday. In the closing address, FIDE President Timur Turlov reflected on the broader significance of a World Championship Match, observing that every such encounter captures the spirit of the era in which it takes place. In this respect, he noted, it is no coincidence that the 2026 edition brings together two exceptionally young representatives of Asian chess powerhouses. He concluded by wishing both contenders the very best of luck before officially declaring the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 open. Written by Yannick Pelletier Photos: Y.E. Nisenbaum and Michal Waluzsa The Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 is taking place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva, Switzerland, from November 22 to December 12. The first round will be played on November 24. All information on the schedule can be found on the Championship website. Tickets to the playing hall and the fan zone can be purchased on the designated website: https://tickets.fide.com/en , while games can be watched on the FIDE YouTube channel with live commentaries by top Grandmasters Peter Leko and Peter Svidler.

title: The two World Championship contenders open up to the media
summary: November 22 marked the official commencement of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026. The assembled journalists were in for a treat, as Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov took part in two separate media sessions, offering insights into their preparations, expectations and thoughts ahead of the eagerly anticipated encounter. The day began at the playing venue, the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, where both contenders met with journalists for a series of individual interviews. Asked about the setting, Sindarov could hardly conceal his admiration: “It is a beautiful room with a fantastic view over the lake!” One thing that quickly became apparent during the exchanges was the high regard in which the two players hold each other. Gukesh was particularly generous in his assessment of his opponent: “He is super talented and energetic, or, in a single word, a genius!” Asked about Gukesh’s recent dip in form, Sindarov offered his own interpretation: “It is true that he has lost quite a lot of games in the past year, but this is because he always tries to win at all costs. I believe that he will be more cautious in the match.” The second part of the media day took place in the afternoon, shortly before the opening ceremony. The press conference was held in Room XIV, also known as the Kazakh Room, at the Palais des Nations in Geneva. Steeped in the history of multilateral diplomacy, the room underwent extensive restoration in 2012 as part of a comprehensive renovation programme at the Palais des Nations. The project was made possible with the support of the then Director-General of the United Nations Office at Geneva, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who is now President of Kazakhstan. Moderated by Grandmaster Maurice Ashley, the official press conference brought together the two World Championship contenders, FIDE President Timur Turlov and H.E. Erzhan Kazykhan, Permanent Representative of Kazakhstan to the United Nations Office and other International Organizations in Geneva. The discussion touched on several interesting aspects of chess’s growing global reach. Timur Turlov noted that the number of people playing chess continues to rise, with digitalisation helping to make the game more accessible, fostering social connections and creating a more level playing field for enthusiasts around the world. Erzhan Kazykhan, for his part, highlighted the strong support chess enjoys from the government in Kazakhstan and across several other Central Asian countries. At a time when everything seems to be getting shorter and faster, both players expressed their deep appreciation for the traditions and unique character of classical World Championship matches. Gukesh described the encounter as a fascinating battle of minds between two players and their respective teams. He also revealed how much he enjoys the training camps ahead of such events, describing them as a source of great fun and positive energy. Sindarov, meanwhile, appeared somewhat more concerned about the psychological demands of the three-week contest. He acknowledged the considerable stress involved and emphasized the importance of finding ways to unwind and recharge between games. When asked about his chances, the challenger admitted that he felt his preparation could have been better and that the seven months between the Candidates Tournament and the World Championship Match had flown by remarkably quickly. Nevertheless, he made it clear that his confidence remained undiminished. Gukesh, for his part, was asked how he intended to cope with the pressure of entering the match as the defending World Champion. His answer left little room for doubt about his mindset: he had not come to Geneva to defend a title but rather to win one. Whether considered the favourite or the underdog, he insisted, his approach would remain unchanged: to give his very best in every game. Written by Yannick Pelletier Photos: Y.E. Nisenbaum and Michal Waluzsa The Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 is taking place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva, Switzerland, from November 22 to December 12. The first round will be played on November 24. All information on the schedule can be found on the Championship website. Tickets to the playing hall and the fan zone can be purchased on the designated website: https://tickets.fide.com/en , while games can be watched on the FIDE YouTube channel with live commentaries by top Grandmasters Peter Leko and Peter Svidler.

title: Total mess in Budapest
summary:
After Magnus Carlsen, the strongest player in the world, once again took liberties in his match against Vladislav Artemiev - this time playing the blitz games and the fast classic game, but skipping the rapid games - one has to conclude that the "pilot" for the Total Chess World Championship has crashed. A commentary. | Photos: Michal Walusza / Total Chess

Total Chess: A false start

It is a pity, really. The Norwegian chess organisers behind the Norway Chess tournaments meant well. They wanted to introduce an exciting new competition format to the world. But they immediately set their sights on the highest possible level: a "Total Chess World Championship". Let us call it, for our German audience, a comprehensive chess world championship. In Germany, we have been somewhat sensitive to terms containing the word "total" ever since 1939. The format even received the blessing of the International Chess Federation because the top two finishers in the series - yes, a series - are supposed to qualify for the Candidates Tournament.

The winner of the series, however, was not to be called Total Chess World Champion - perhaps that sounded a little too much like world domination even for FIDE. Instead, the title would be "World Combined Champion" . That sounds a little like skiing, but it does describe the concept, since the basic idea is to combine different disciplines.

Magnus Carlsen as the guiding spirit

We all know that Magnus Carlsen, the great dominant force in chess for the past 15 years, the GOAT (Greatest of All Time), has somewhat lost his enthusiasm for classical chess. It takes a great deal of time, and modern computer-assisted opening preparation also allows players who are clearly weaker in their understanding of the game to keep pace with him for a long time and perhaps even land the occasional "lucky punch". For this reason, Carlsen did not defend his world title and has also become increasingly scarce at tournaments with long time controls. He had still negotiated with FIDE about whether the World Championship format could be changed in the direction now being implemented in the Total Chess World Championship. Carlsen is therefore, in a sense, the guiding spirit behind the idea and probably had some involvement in shaping the tournament as well.

Classical chess is, after all, a rather valuable asset. For almost 200 years, tournament games have been recorded and published. The world's best players have always been great artists and have created genuine works of art with their games, works that contemporaries and later generations could enjoy and learn from. Magnus Carlsen stands very much in that tradition. But the Norwegian is also someone who constantly seeks challenges and loves the thrill of games at short and very short time controls. He has played countless Blitz and Bullet games and is now the world champion in a number of formats. A book entitled "All the Games of Magnus Carlsen" will never exist - it would simply be far too extensive.

The sheer number of top-level games played nowadays, especially in online tournaments, also has some disadvantages. The contemplative aspect is completely lost amid the flood of Blitz and Rapid games. One Rapid or Blitz game is immediately followed by the next. Everything rushes past, and chess fans have no time to engage more deeply with the games, enjoy them and think about them. This effect can already be observed even with classical games. Chess is incredibly popular, and one tournament follows another. Some chess fans feel oversaturated.

And so the top GMs play countless games against one another and by now know each other inside out: their opening repertoires, their strengths and their weaknesses. After the 50 th or 100 th game against the same opponent, one can perhaps become a little tired and bored.

A new format with birth defects

It was in this situation that the Norwegians launched their Total Chess World Championship - though with a whole series of "birth defects".

The basic idea itself, a mixture of three time-control formats, is probably not particularly convincing. One wonders: what exactly is the point? Is it not enough simply to hold tournaments at one time control or another? There is a classical World Championship, but also a Blitz World Championship and a Rapid World Championship.

In Total Chess, blitz games, rapid games and classical games are played on the same day, and the results are added together according to some formula.

Because playing a genuine classical tournament game alongside blitz and rapid games on the same day would presumably have been too much of a good thing, the time control was cut in half: 45 instead of 90 minutes of base time. But that is an enormous difference for the players. They have some time to think, but not enough for deep calculation. Some players have pointed this out as well. Playing through games at all the different time controls on a single day also appears to overburden and tire the players.

FIDE has already experimented in the past with shorter semi-classical time controls and counts the results towards the classical Elo rating. That is not a good idea! Games with 45 minutes and games with 90 minutes are two very different things. The Total Chess organisers also want to develop a Total Chess rating list. Oh dear, yet another Elo rating. There is already classical Elo, Rapid Elo and Blitz Elo. Is that not enough? Some chess fans already find Rapid and Blitz ratings rather unnecessary.

Totally complicated

Next, the Total Chess organisers devised a complicated set of regulations and a scoring system for their tournament. To understand it in full, one really needs to have studied two semesters of chess tournament science. Chess is normally so simple: if you win, you get the point. If you lose, the other player gets the point. If the game is drawn, the point is shared. Simple and good. Everyone understands it immediately, even non-chess players.

The Total Chess World Championship was conceived as a series of three tournaments with 24 players and a final featuring the top four. The chess calendar is already packed with tournaments. Now an entire additional series involving 24 top players is being squeezed into it. Those players will then be unavailable elsewhere. There will be plenty of clashes with other tournaments.

FIDE once ran a Grand Prix series as a qualification route for the Candidates Tournament. There too, more or less the same players met one another over the course of the year. There was also a points system, just as in the Total Chess World Championship. The top two then qualified for the Candidates Tournament. What happened in the FIDE Grand Prix events was that after two or three tournaments only a few players still had a chance of earning one of the qualifying places. The other players then lost interest and no longer wanted to take part. FIDE had to fill the tournaments with players from a reserve list, which distorted the results and devalued the series. In the end, FIDE was right to abandon it.

Holes in the regulations

Despite their length, the Total Chess World Championship regulations apparently still contain major loopholes, which Magnus Carlsen has exploited in an unsporting manner, unfortunately that is what one has to call it. The idea is that the players compete in blitz, rapid and semi-classical chess across two matches. Against Bibisara Assaubayeva, Carlsen had already built such a large lead after the blitz and rapid games that he could no longer be caught. He then simply did not show up for the semi-classical game. That is obviously not acceptable and would be completely unthinkable in other sports. Why does Carlsen do this? Unsporting behaviour is not something one normally associates with him.

Normally, Carlsen could simply have played a few token moves in the unnecessary game and agreed a draw, but that was no longer an option for him. Because of his poor results in the semi-classical games during the round-robin part of the event - no wins and one loss - Carlsen had damaged his Elo rating and was in danger not only of falling below 2800, but perhaps even of losing his long-held position as world number one. As mentioned: FIDE rates these shorter long games as genuine classical games. Carlsen, however, seems to have problems with this time control. In any case, he is not as dominant as usual. From Carlsen's point of view, a draw or a loss against Assaubayeva would have been a disaster.

Several other players followed Carlsen's example and also sat out the long games. Of course: if the "boss" does it, the others will do it too.

In Thursday's round, Carlsen then did not play the rapid games against Artemiev. Why now? Carlsen was ahead after the blitz games and had calculated that a win against Artemiev in the semi-classical game (worth 8 points) would be enough to win the match, while also being important for repairing his classical Elo rating. Carlsen later explained that he wanted to save his energy for the longer game as well.

Total Chess: A total write-off?

It was a good thing that the Norwegians held a pilot tournament for their Total Chess World Championship series. They can now investigate the causes of the crash and perhaps repair the format. But perhaps it is simply a total write-off.

title: LIVE: The World Championship kicks off – press conference and opening ceremony today
summary:
Gukesh Dommaraju faces Javokhir Sindarov in the 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship in Geneva. The first move will be played on Tuesday, 24 November, at 15:00 CET. Today, the players will meet the press at 15:30, followed by the opening ceremony at 17:00 CET. | Live coverage today: Press conference: 15:30 CET, 9:30 EST  | Opening ceremony: 17:00 CET, 11:00 EST | Images: FIDE

The 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship in Geneva finally gets underway today with the official press conference, featuring the two World Championship contenders, host Maurice Ashley and FIDE President Timur Turlov, followed 90 minutes later by the opening ceremony.

Live coverage of the press conference on FIDE's YouTube channel from 15:30 CET

Live coverage of the opening ceremony on FIDE's YouTube channel from 17:00 CET

Links

Javokhir Sindarov - The next World Champion?

The difficult road to defending his title: Gukesh Dommaraju

Official website of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship

World Championship side events

FIDE on YouTube

Information about the 2026 World Chess Championship

Format: 14 classical games

Starting time: Daily at 3 p.m. local time

Playing dates: 24 Nov, 25 Nov, 26 Nov, 28 Nov, 29 Nov, 30 Nov, 2 Dec, 3 Dec, 4 Dec, 6 Dec, 7 Dec, 8 Dec, 10 Dec, 11 Dec. Tiebreaks/award ceremony: 12 Dec

Rest days: 27 Nov, 1 Dec, 5 Dec, 9 Dec

Official opening: 22 Nov

Venue: Fondation Martin Bodmer , Route Martin-Bodmer 19, 1223 Cologny

Tickets: Information and booking

Early conclusion: If one player takes an unassailable lead, the remaining games will not be played. This happens when a player reaches 7½ points.

Time control: 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game, with a 30-second increment per move from move 41

Draw rule: No draw offers before Black's 40th move. Exceptions apply in cases of threefold repetition and stalemate

Tiebreak: First, four rapid games (15 minutes plus 10 seconds per move), followed by two games at 10+5 and then two blitz games at 3+2. If the score is still tied, further blitz games at 3+2 will be played until a winner emerges. Colours will be drawn before each new tiebreak stage. A 10-minute break is scheduled between games

Prize fund: US$2.5 million. In principle, each player receives $200,000 for every point scored through a game victory. The remaining amount is split. Special rules apply to certain final scores involving a particularly high number of decisive games and to a victory in the tiebreaks

Media regulations: Both players are required, among other things, to attend daily press conferences after their games and take part in at least two promotional events

Source: FIDE: Regulations for the FIDE World Championship Match 2026

Live commentary

Peter Leko and Peter Svidler are the official commentators for the 2026 FIDE World Championship match between Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva.

Watch the live coverage on FIDE's YouTube channel
